It's November 2034. The company that owns the building of the café “Bei Ingrid” wants to raise the rent by 60% from January. Lena is talking on the phone with Mrs Berger, the company's representative.
Mrs Berger, I've received your letter. Sixty per cent more rent from January. For a small café that just isn't feasible.
Mrs Brandt, I understand your situation. But I represent the owners' interests here. Commercial rents in Prenzlauer Berg have risen sharply over the last ten years. Your rent is well below average.
I have to contradict you there. When I signed the contract, the premises had been empty for two years. Nobody wanted them. I renovated them, with my own money.
That may be. I agree with you insofar as you've increased the value of the premises. But that's exactly why they're worth more now.
So I'm being punished for turning an empty space into a place where the whole street meets?
I wouldn't put it like that. But I understand your point of view. What do you suggest?
How about a compromise? Twenty per cent more, spread over three years. And a ten-year contract.
Twenty per cent is too little. I can't propose that to the owners. Forty would be the minimum.
Then I'd have to close. Mrs Berger, I understand you're doing your job. But could you at least pass on to the owners what this café means for the neighbourhood?
I can do that. But I'm not promising anything. You have until the end of December to decide.

The news spread faster than any of Mrs Becker's rumours. By the evening, after Lena had spoken to Mrs Berger on the phone, half of Kastanienallee knew. By the next morning, all of it. The café “Bei Ingrid” was going to close. The very café where for four years, every morning at seven, the first workers drank their coffee, where Mrs Schulze sat every afternoon at her table by the window, where Grete did crosswords with Ludwig, where Andrei baked bread at four in the morning and the children were allowed to ring the brass bell. Elif cried when she heard. Then she went to her room, took the clipboard she had kept from collecting signatures for Ingrid-Brandt-Platz and started a new list.

Lena herself said almost nothing for two days. She opened the café every morning at seven as usual, baked with Andrei, served the customers, smiled. But in the evenings she sat for a long time in the empty kitchen, in front of a sheet of paper on which she worked out figures, again and again: rent, electricity, flour, butter, wages. However she turned it, with the rent sixty per cent higher the café would have gone bankrupt within six months. Andrei found her there on the second evening, at eleven, bent over the figures, her eyes red. He sat down next to her and said nothing. Then he took the pen out of her hand. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we ask the street. You've fed the street for four years. Now it's time for the street to help you for once.”

Three days later there was a meeting. Not in the café, it was too small, but in Ingrid's Reading Corner, on the ground floor of number thirty-three, among the bookshelves, cushions and the old armchair by the window. More than sixty people came. They sat on chairs, on cushions, on the floor, stood between the shelves. Mrs Krause from the district office had come, even though she wasn't responsible for commercial rents, “in a private capacity”, as she stressed. Michael Kühn had come from Munich because Lena had called him. And Katrin Krüger sat in the back row with her notebook, and this time she was taking notes.

Grete had come too, in her wheelchair, pushed by Mara, who was six months pregnant and wouldn't be stopped. Grete didn't say a word all evening. But she kept Elif's clipboard on her knees the whole time, like a guard.

Andrei had prepared a chart, on a big screen he had borrowed from the BVG office. It showed how commercial rents in Prenzlauer Berg had developed from 2024 to 2034. The red line climbed steeply, from eleven euros per square metre to twenty-two. “Rents have doubled in ten years,” Andrei explained, in the calm tone of his BVG presentations. “In the same period, seven small shops closed in our neighbourhood: two bakeries, a bookshop, a shoemaker, a florist, a toy shop and the café on the corner of Oderberger Straße. In their place there are now three chains and four holiday flats. From this we can conclude that it's not about one single café. It's about the question of who a street belongs to.”

It was a long discussion. Not everyone agreed. A young man who had lived on the street for a year and worked at a start-up said he didn't really understand the fuss: the owners had the right to make money with their property, that's how the market works. “I have to contradict you there,” said Mrs Krause calmly, and everyone turned round. “I agree with you insofar as it's legal. But not everything that's legal is also wise. A street with nothing left but chains and holiday flats will at some point be a street where nobody wants to live any more. Not even you.” The young man thought about it. Then he said: “That may be. But what's the solution?”

There were suggestions. A woman proposed setting up a cooperative and buying the building, but Andrei quickly worked out that it would cost more than three million euros. A man proposed demonstrating in front of the owners' house, but nobody knew where the owners lived; it was a company based in Luxembourg. Elif stood up with her clipboard and said she had already collected eight hundred signatures, in two days, at the stop. Everyone applauded. But Mrs Krause said quietly what everyone was thinking: “Signatures help at the district office. Unfortunately they don't help with a company in Luxembourg.”

At that moment Michael stood up. He had stood silently by the wall the whole time, next to the photo of Ingrid that hung above the armchair. He cleared his throat. “I have a proposal,” he said. “On the ground floor of this building, on the other side of the hallway, there's a room that has been empty since the summer. There used to be a tailor's there. It's bigger than the current café, with two windows onto the street and a door to the courtyard. And it's right on Ingrid-Brandt-Platz. I'll rent it to Lena. At the rent she pays now. With a twenty-year contract.”

The Reading Corner went quiet. Lena looked at Michael as if she hadn't heard him properly. “Michael,” she said quietly, “I can't accept. You'll lose money on this. A lot of money. You could rent the space out for twice as much.” Michael smiled. “Mrs Brandt, your grandmother made me cocoa every afternoon and taught me to read without taking a pfennig for it. A whole year. I've worked out what that would cost today, tutoring every day for a year. It's roughly what I'll lose in rent over twenty years. Don't see it as a gift. See it as a repayment. Thirty years late.”

Lena couldn't say anything. She looked at her grandfather, who was sitting in the front row, on the best chair, which Elif had reserved for him. Ludwig nodded slowly. Then he said, loud enough for everyone to hear: “I hold the view that you don't turn down an offer like that. Ingrid would have said: anyone who gives for years has to learn to receive as well. Otherwise it isn't generosity, it's pride.” A few people laughed. Lena wiped her eyes. “On one condition,” she said to Michael. “The children from the Reading Corner get a free cocoa every afternoon. For ever.” Michael held out his hand. “I can live with that,” he said.

That evening Katrin Krüger wrote an article, which appeared two days later in the Berliner Zeitung under the headline “Ein Café zieht um – und bleibt” (A café moves – and stays). She quoted Mrs Krause, Andrei, the young man from the start-up, who at the end had offered to program the café's new website for free, and Elif, who said she had learned for the second time that a list of signatures doesn't always change something, but that the people who sign always change something. The article was read all over Berlin. In the following weeks, three more property owners from Prenzlauer Berg got in touch with Mrs Krause and asked whether there were small shops in their buildings too that they could rent out at fair rents. “Michael has started something,” Mrs Krause said to Ludwig. “I don't know what yet. But it's catching.”

Shortly before Christmas, Mrs Berger called once more. Lena was expecting one last negotiation, a new offer, maybe a threat. Instead, after a long pause, Mrs Berger said, in a voice that suddenly no longer sounded like a company: “Mrs Brandt, I've read the article. I've lived in Prenzlauer Berg for twenty years. My son used to play football on your street. Actually I'm not allowed to say this. But I'm glad you've found a solution. I really am.” Lena invited her to the opening. Mrs Berger said that unfortunately that wasn't possible, for professional reasons. On the first of January she came anyway, the fifth customer, and ordered a cocoa.

The café moved on the last weekend of December, between Christmas and New Year's Eve. The whole street helped. Mr Yilmaz and his colleagues from the BVG carried the tables. Leo, in the second year of his apprenticeship, came in uniform straight from a shift and carried the espresso machine, which was heavier than he thought. Kuba and Ola painted the walls of the former tailor's a warm yellow, chosen by Lena because it was the colour of the light in Ingrid's living room. Andrei installed a new oven in the bakery. And Ludwig sat on a chair in the middle of the empty room giving instructions that nobody followed, and he was happy.

At the very end, when everything was in its place, Lena took the old brass bell out of a box and hung it next to the new till. Next to the bell she hung the printed email from the woman in Spandau who had visited her sister with Andrei's app. Beside it, the photo of Ingrid that had hung for years in the old café. And underneath, a new little sign, painted by Elif in her round handwriting: “Cocoa for the children from the Reading Corner: free. For ever.” On the first of January 2035, at seven in the morning, the café “Bei Ingrid” opened for the first time in its new place, right on Ingrid-Brandt-Platz, looking out onto a step-free stop and a young chestnut tree. The first customer was Ludwig. He ordered a coffee, sat down by the window and rang the bell. Once. For everyone who had helped.
